strengths: The problem has an identifiable audience in contextual bandits, Bayesian optimization, and resource allocation. Combining changing arm availability with combinatorial semi-bandit feedback is practically relevant.

The GP-UCB and approximation-oracle framework is clearly motivated. The monotonicity/Lipschitz regret decomposition, batch covariance analysis, and information-gain maximization over feasible arrival sequences provide useful theoretical components.

The experiments examine covariance variation and two data-derived applications, report five runs with standard deviations, and demonstrate useful performance/runtime tradeoffs between exact and sparse GP implementations.
weaknesses: Necessary—repair the adaptive-design argument supporting Theorem 1. In Appendix A, equations (16)–(17), a deterministic oracle does not make selected contexts nonrandom: selections depend on random observations. Consequently, the stated unconditional mutual information cannot simply equal a realization-dependent log-determinant without further justification. A pathwise determinant argument for each realized feasible design could repair this, but the manuscript must establish that connection. Also, squaring the approximation regret in equation (22) requires handling its potentially negative sign.

Necessary—correct the kernel-specific scaling and information-gain definition. Substituting the cited Matérn information-gain bound into Theorem 1 gives, up to logarithms, sqrt(λ*(K)+σ²) times (KT)^((D+ν)/(D+2ν)). Corollary 1 retains only sqrt(K), omitting an additional polynomial dependence on K; Table 1 gives another inconsistent expression. Furthermore, equation (4) depends on per-round availability and feasibility, whereas the following text incorrectly identifies it with ordinary maximum information gain over the union of contexts.

Necessary—make the application models mathematically well defined and distinguish them from the theorem's assumptions. In Simulation I, log(1+sum r_i) can be undefined under Gaussian observation noise, and its compatibility with the reward assumptions is unexplained. Simulation III uses Bernoulli feedback and constructed activation probabilities, outside the stated GP-sample/Gaussian-noise model. It also does not explain how unbounded GP-UCB indices are converted into valid probabilities for TIM+. These can be legitimate heuristic experiments, but their actual implementation and relationship to the guarantees need clarification.

Necessary—resolve experimental specification inconsistencies. Simulation I specifies 250 rounds but configures CC-MAB using 300, and lists inducing-point counts of 10, 20, and 50 while reporting results for 100 as well. The sparse implementation needs a clearer account of whether all observations enter the variational fit, how hyperparameters are treated, and what computation is included in timing. These details matter for reproducing the reported accuracy and speedups.

Necessary—narrow conclusions to the evidence supplied. MovieLens outcomes are generated from a prescribed context-to-probability function, so this is a semi-synthetic evaluation. Matching its randomized approximate-oracle benchmark does not establish the 'optimal performance' claimed in Section 5.3.3. Comparisons against ACC-UCB and CC-MAB support gains over those baselines, rather than the broad superiority claim over previous UCB methods, particularly given the closely related GP work discussed in Section 1.2. Likewise, Figure 4's hundreds of seconds per sparse update at 250 rounds do not establish general online scalability. Narrower claims would address these concerns without requiring state-of-the-art results.
Optional—kernel-misspecification sensitivity and a concrete example quantifying the improvement from arrival-constrained information gain would make the findings easier to interpret and apply.
